courses.title: Biomedical Signal Processing
courses.description: Origin and characteristics of biosignals, sampling and digitisation, filtering, frequency analysis, and processing of ECG, EEG and EMG.

topics.title: Biosignals and Acquisition
topics.summary: Types of biosignals, amplitude and frequency ranges, electrodes and amplifiers.

material.heading: Characteristics
material.body: Biosignals are measurable quantities reflecting physiological activity: bioelectric (ECG from the heart — about 0.5–4 mV, 0.05–150 Hz diagnostic bandwidth; EEG from the brain — 10–100 µV, 0.5–100 Hz; EMG from muscles — 0.1–5 mV, 20–500 Hz or more; EOG from eye movement), biomechanical (blood pressure, respiration), biochemical (glucose, oxygen saturation) and bioacoustic (heart sounds). Signals may be deterministic or random, stationary or non-stationary (most biosignals are non-stationary). Sources of noise and artefacts: power-line interference (50 Hz in Nigeria), baseline wander (respiration, movement), muscle (EMG) artefact, electrode motion artefact and electromagnetic interference.

material.heading: Electrodes and amplifiers
material.body: Silver/silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) electrodes are non-polarisable, giving stable low-noise recordings; electrode gel reduces skin impedance. Biopotential amplifiers must have high input impedance (to avoid loading the source), high common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR > 80–100 dB — rejecting interference common to both inputs such as mains hum), appropriate gain (e.g. 1,000 for ECG) and bandwidth, and patient isolation for electrical safety. The instrumentation amplifier (three op-amp configuration) is the standard differential front end. The right-leg drive circuit feeds back inverted common-mode voltage to the body to reduce interference. Anti-aliasing low-pass filters precede digitisation.

topics.title: Sampling and Digitisation
topics.summary: Nyquist theorem, aliasing, quantisation and analogue-to-digital conversion.

material.heading: Sampling
material.body: Analogue signals are converted into discrete-time digital signals by sampling at regular intervals. The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem states that the sampling frequency must be at least twice the highest frequency present in the signal (fs ≥ 2fmax) to reconstruct it without loss; half the sampling rate is the Nyquist frequency. Sampling below this causes aliasing — high frequencies appear falsely as lower frequencies — prevented by an analogue anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the ADC. In practice, oversampling (e.g. ECG at 250–1,000 Hz, EMG at 1–2 kHz or more) is used.

material.heading: Quantisation and ADC
material.body: Quantisation assigns each sample to one of a finite number of levels determined by ADC resolution (n bits → 2^n levels). The quantisation step size (LSB) = input range / 2^n; quantisation error introduces noise, and the signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio improves by about 6 dB per bit. Typical biomedical ADCs use 12–24 bits (sigma–delta converters for high resolution at low frequencies). Other ADC types: successive approximation (common, moderate speed) and flash (fastest). Digital signals are stored and processed as sequences x[n]; the sampling interval T = 1/fs.

topics.title: Digital Filtering
topics.summary: FIR and IIR filters, filter types, notch filters and moving average.

material.heading: Filter types
material.body: Filters remove unwanted components: low-pass (removes high-frequency noise such as muscle artefact), high-pass (removes baseline wander — e.g. 0.5 Hz cut-off for monitoring ECG, 0.05 Hz for diagnostic ECG to preserve ST segments), band-pass (retains a frequency band — e.g. QRS detection 5–15 Hz) and band-stop/notch (removes a narrow band such as 50 Hz mains interference). Filter characteristics include cut-off frequency (−3 dB point), passband ripple, transition band, stopband attenuation, order (steepness) and phase response. Filtering must preserve clinically important features — aggressive high-pass filtering distorts ST segments and can mimic ischaemia.

material.heading: FIR and IIR
material.body: Finite impulse response (FIR) filters use only current and past inputs (y[n] = Σ bk x[n−k]); they are always stable and can have exactly linear phase (no waveform distortion), but need higher orders. The moving average filter is a simple FIR low-pass filter. Infinite impulse response (IIR) filters also use past outputs (feedback), achieving sharp responses with lower order, but may be unstable and have non-linear phase; designs include Butterworth (maximally flat passband), Chebyshev (steeper with ripple) and elliptic. Zero-phase filtering (forward–backward filtering, e.g. filtfilt) removes phase distortion offline. Adaptive filters (LMS algorithm) track changing noise, e.g. removing maternal ECG from fetal ECG or mains interference with a reference input.

topics.title: Frequency and Time–Frequency Analysis
topics.summary: Fourier transform, FFT, power spectrum, windowing, and wavelets.

material.heading: Fourier analysis
material.body: The Fourier transform decomposes signals into sinusoidal components, revealing frequency content. The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) applies to sampled signals; the fast Fourier transform (FFT, Cooley–Tukey) computes it efficiently (N log N rather than N² operations). Frequency resolution = fs / N (longer records give finer resolution). The power spectral density shows power distribution across frequencies — e.g. EEG bands: delta (< 4 Hz, deep sleep), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz, relaxed awake with eyes closed), beta (13–30 Hz, active thinking) and gamma (> 30 Hz). Heart rate variability analysis uses spectral bands (LF, HF) reflecting autonomic balance. Windowing (Hamming, Hanning) reduces spectral leakage from truncating signals.
keyPoints: EEG bands: delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma

material.heading: Time–frequency methods
material.body: Because biosignals are non-stationary, time–frequency methods show how frequency content changes over time. The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) applies FFT to short sliding windows, producing a spectrogram, with a fixed trade-off between time and frequency resolution. The wavelet transform uses scaled and shifted wavelets (e.g. Daubechies, Morlet), giving good time resolution at high frequencies and good frequency resolution at low frequencies — useful for detecting transients (QRS complexes, epileptic spikes) and for denoising and compression. Other techniques: autocorrelation (periodicity), cross-correlation (similarity/time delay between signals), principal and independent component analysis (ICA — removing eye-blink artefacts from EEG).

topics.title: Applications: ECG, EEG and EMG Processing
topics.summary: QRS detection, heart rate variability, seizure detection, EMG analysis and wearables.

material.heading: ECG and EEG
material.body: Automated ECG analysis begins with QRS detection; the Pan–Tompkins algorithm uses band-pass filtering (5–15 Hz), differentiation, squaring, moving-window integration and adaptive thresholds. R–R intervals give heart rate and heart rate variability (time-domain measures: SDNN, RMSSD). Arrhythmia classification increasingly uses machine learning and deep learning (e.g. atrial fibrillation detection by smartwatches). ST segment analysis detects ischaemia. EEG processing supports seizure detection, sleep staging, depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring (bispectral index), and brain–computer interfaces. Event-related potentials are extracted by ensemble averaging, improving SNR by √N.

material.heading: EMG and wearables
material.body: Surface EMG features include root mean square (RMS) amplitude and integrated EMG (muscle activation level), median and mean frequency (fall with fatigue), and onset detection. Needle EMG and nerve conduction studies diagnose neuromuscular disease. EMG signals control myoelectric prosthetic hands via pattern recognition. Wearable and mobile health devices (smartwatches, patches, low-cost ECG devices) acquire biosignals continuously with limited power, requiring efficient algorithms, motion-artefact handling, data compression and secure transmission. Photoplethysmography (PPG) measures pulse and oxygen saturation (pulse oximetry uses red and infrared light absorption ratios). Validation against gold standards and regulatory approval are essential before clinical use.
